title: Viral Hook Examples: 40 Openers Built for the First Three Seconds
markdown:
# Viral Hook Examples: 40 Openers Built for the First Three Seconds

At 0:02, a thumb pauses over your video, then keeps moving. The footage may be good; the first spoken line simply gave the viewer no reason to stay.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/NW5TFTuEOj.png)

This page gives you 40 viral hook examples you can adapt without inventing results. Pick one that matches the tension in your video, make the payoff specific, then test it against another opening.

## Contrarian viral hook examples

Use these when you can challenge a familiar assumption and explain the exception immediately.

1. “Stop trying to [common goal] this way.”
2. “The advice everyone gives about [topic] is backwards.”
3. “You do not need more [tool]; you need this first.”
4. “I would not start [activity] with [popular first step].”
5. “The fastest way to make [problem] worse is [common behavior].”
6. “More effort is not the answer to [problem].”
7. “Before you buy [thing], watch this.”
8. “The ‘right’ way to [goal] is why beginners quit.”

## Question hooks

Questions work when the viewer can answer internally before you reveal the answer.

9. “Why does [problem] happen right after you [action]?”
10. “What would change if you stopped doing [habit] for seven days?”
11. “Are you making this [topic] mistake without noticing?”
12. “Why do most people get stuck at this exact step?”
13. “Which of these [two options] would you choose?”
14. “Can you spot what is wrong in this [screen/result/setup]?”
15. “What is actually costing you [time/money/energy] here?”
16. “Why does [desired outcome] feel harder than it should?”

## Mistake hooks

Make the mistake recognizable, then give a useful correction rather than a vague warning.

17. “You are not bad at [skill]. You are starting in the wrong place.”
18. “This is the [topic] mistake I see beginners make first.”
19. “If [bad result] keeps happening, check this before anything else.”
20. “You fixed the symptom, not the reason [problem] keeps returning.”
21. “Do not copy this [popular tactic] until you know this.”
22. “The tiny setup mistake that makes [task] take twice as long.”
23. “Your [result] is not inconsistent—your process is.”
24. “If your [project] feels messy, this is probably missing.”

## Before-and-after hooks

Use a visible contrast. If you use a number, replace the blank with a number you can verify.

25. “This took [ADD: your time] before I changed one step.”
26. “From [before state] to [after state]: here is what changed.”
27. “I rebuilt this [thing] with one rule: [rule].”
28. “The difference between version one and version two is not what you think.”
29. “This is what [problem] looks like before the fix.”
30. “I removed [thing] from this workflow. Here is what happened next.”
31. “Watch this [process] go from [before] to [after].”
32. “One small change made this result easier to repeat.”

## Story and reveal hooks

Start in the middle of a moment, then make the viewer need the missing context.

33. “I knew this [plan/process] was failing when [specific moment].”
34. “This looked like a win until I checked [detail].”
35. “I almost deleted this because [reason].”
36. “The first sign I had chosen the wrong [tool/approach] was this.”
37. “Here is the part nobody shows when they teach [topic].”
38. “I tried the obvious solution first. It failed for one reason.”
39. “This is the moment [result] finally made sense.”
40. “I thought [assumption], until this happened.”

## How to choose a hook

Choose the opening by the job your video needs to do.

- Use a contrarian hook when viewers already know the usual advice.
- Use a question when the video answers one sharp uncertainty.
- Use a mistake hook when you can diagnose and correct a familiar failure.
- Use a before-and-after hook when the visual change is real and visible.
- Use a story hook when the lesson needs context to matter.

Keep the first line aligned with the actual video. A hook that promises a secret but delivers a general tip may earn a pause and lose trust. The next sentence should narrow the promise: name the mistake, show the comparison, or begin the first step.

## How to test viral hook examples

Test two openings on the same underlying idea before you change everything else. Keep the topic, footage, length, and takeaway as similar as you can. Change the first spoken line and the first on-screen text.

A practical sequence is:

1. Write three hooks from different types—for example, one question, one contrarian line, and one mistake.
2. Make the opening visual support the exact line.
3. Put the explanation or proof immediately after the hook.
4. Review which opening creates the clearest expectation for the rest of the video.
5. Keep the winner only if the content actually delivers what it promised.

The goal is not to sound dramatic. It is to make the right viewer understand, in a few seconds, why this particular video is worth their attention.

## FAQ

### What makes a good short-form video hook?

A good hook states a specific tension, question, mistake, contrast, or outcome that the video resolves. It should be understandable without extra context and matched by the next beat of the video.

### Should the spoken hook and on-screen text be identical?

Not always. They can reinforce the same idea from two angles. For example, the spoken line can name the problem while the on-screen text names the mistake.

### How many hooks should I write for one video?

Write at least three. Different hook types reveal different angles in the same material, and a comparison gives you a clearer choice than settling on the first line.

### Can I use these examples in any niche?

Yes, if you replace the brackets with a concrete topic and keep the claim honest. A finance, fitness, food, software, or creator video still needs a promise it can fulfill.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the input and the structured output you receive:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
